Sukkot. The Feast of Tabernacles is a seven-day festival beginning on the fifteenth of Tishrei, in September or October. It commemorates the Israelites' wandering in the desert after the Exodus and celebrates the autumn harvest, marked by dwelling in temporary booths called sukkot and using the four species of plants in ritual observance.

Sukkot are small, temporary structures with roofs made of branches and vegetation, symbolizing the dwellings used during the desert wandering. Living in and eating in the sukkah is meant to inspire gratitude and humility, reminding Jews of reliance on God's protection and provision. The lulav and etrog, a bound bundle of palm, willow, and myrtle branches alongside a citron fruit, are shaken in all directions during morning prayers. The four species are said to represent different parts of the Jewish community and the importance of unity.

The holiday blends commemoration of ancient wanderings with a joyful harvest festival, making it one of the most celebratory Jewish holidays. Simchat Torah, the Rejoicing of the Law, occurs at the end of Sukkot and marks the conclusion and immediate restart of Torah reading for the year. A secondary observance, Hoshana Rabbah, the seventh day, features additional processionals and water libations that developed through rabbinic tradition. Historically, Sukkot was one of the three pilgrimage festivals when Jews would travel to the Temple in Jerusalem, paired with Passover, another pilgrimage festival commemorating the Exodus, and completing the triad of major pilgrimage festivals with Shavuot.
